Gaslighting.short_definition: Repeatedly denying what someone saw, heard or remembers until they stop trusting their own account of events.
Gaslighting.core_meaning: Repeatedly denying what someone saw, heard or remembers until they stop trusting their own account of events.
Gaslighting.expanded_definition: Gaslighting is a pattern of contradicting a person's memory or perception, often about things that clearly happened, so that they begin to defer to the other person's version of events. One denial means little. The pattern shows when the contradiction repeats, targets things the person has good reason to be sure of, and follows moments when they raised a concern. Over time the person may start double-checking themselves instead of the situation.
Gaslighting.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps telling you that what you clearly remember didn't happen, until you start wondering whether you can trust your own mind.
Gaslighting.why_this_matters: When you can't rely on your own memory, you lose the ability to say what happened, notice a pattern, or ask for change. Naming the pattern accurately, without overclaiming, usually helps more than either ignoring it or assuming the worst.
what_it_is: Contradicting something you witnessed or lived through, flatly, with no room left for an honest mistake.
Recasting your reaction as the problem: you are too sensitive, too emotional, or confused.
Repeating this across many topics and many weeks, so doubt builds up instead of being settled.
Aimed most often at the moments you raise a concern or point to evidence, such as a saved message or something said in front of others.
what_it_sounds_like: I never said that. You're making it up.
You know how you get. You always twist things.
Everyone else agrees with me. You're the only one who sees it that way.
I'm worried about you. You've been so confused lately.
what_it_is_not: Two people recalling a long-ago conversation differently, and both willing to check a text or ask someone else.
A single correction of a small detail, such as which night a dinner was or who said what at a party.
Someone saying 'I see it differently' about how an event felt, which is a difference of view and not a denial of the facts.
Plain forgetting. Memory fades and merges events, and an honest 'I don't remember that' is not an attack on yours.
Disagreeing with your explanation of why something happened while accepting that it did happen.
this_may_be_it_when: The thing being denied is something you can back up with a message, a receipt, or a witness.
The denial arrives with a comment about you: your memory, your stability, or your habit of exaggerating.
It happens when you raise a complaint and almost never when the topic is neutral.
An offer to look at the evidence together is refused or turned into an argument.
You have started keeping notes or screenshots, not to use them, but to reassure yourself that you are not wrong.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The topic is something neither of you recorded, and both of you admit you may be mixing it up.
They suggest looking at the message or asking a third person, and then accept what it shows.
It happened once, in a stressful week, and has not come back.
The doubt is about your interpretation of an event, not about whether it took place.
They correct themselves too, with something like 'I got that wrong earlier'.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Stress, tiredness and a crowded week blur memory for everyone, including you.
Two people notice different parts of the same scene and honestly describe different events.
Someone defensive in the moment may deny something and then admit it hours later.
common_false_positives: A friend who corrects the date of a trip once, and is happy to be shown otherwise.
A partner who truly does not recall a conversation that took place while they were distracted or half asleep.
A family argument in which each side retells a past event with the details that suit their feelings, and nobody is trying to shake anyone else's grip on reality.
discernment_questions: Is there something you could both look at, such as a message or a calendar entry, and would they agree to look?
When the evidence is shown, does the denial change, or does the subject?
Does the doubt attach to your memory in general, or to one disputed detail?
Do you feel less sure of yourself with this person than with others who knew the same events?
Would a neutral person who saw the same evidence side with their version or yours?
less_concerning_if: The disagreement is about something genuinely unrecorded, and both of you stay open to being wrong.
They accept the evidence when it is shown, even grudgingly.
You feel as confident about your memory around other people as you do around this one.
more_concerning_if: The denial covers things with clear proof and carries on after the proof is shown.
Your confidence has dropped across areas of life, not only in this relationship.
They tell other people that you have been confused or unwell, so that your account is discounted before you give it.
pattern_over_time_signs: You rehearse what you will say before raising anything, because you expect to be told it did not happen.
You check your memory against screenshots or notes more often than you used to.
You apologize first, even when you are not sure what for.
Friends or family who knew you before have remarked that you seem less sure of yourself.
Gaslighting.repair_check: After you show the evidence, what happens next tells you. If they say plainly that you were right about that, and answer differently the next time it comes up, something has changed. One apology followed by the same denial next week has not.
Gaslighting.boundary_respect_check: Ask to look at the message together and watch what follows. Someone who respects the request opens it with you. Someone who does not turns the conversation toward whether you can be trusted to remember anything.
Gaslighting.psychological_mechanism: Repeated contradiction can move where a person places their trust, from their own sense of what happened to the other person's account. It tends to work best where the person depends on the other for approval, housing or belonging, and when the denial arrives calmly and with apparent concern. Over time, checking the other person's version can become a habit.
Gaslighting.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe second-guessing themselves, keeping private records, avoiding the disputed topic, and finding it harder to make decisions. Some describe relief on learning the pattern has a name, and some describe anger at how long it went unnamed.

response_options.soft_clarification: State what you remember in one sentence and ask for a shared check: 'I remember it differently. Can we look at the thread together?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to debate whether your memory works: 'I'm not going to argue about whether I remember my own life correctly. I'm happy to look at what we wrote.'
response_options.disengagement: End the conversation when it moves from the event to you, and return to the subject only in writing or with a third person present.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe two or three specific examples to someone who knew you before this relationship and see whether your account rings true to them. An outside view helps you test your own.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, confirm decisions in writing right after meetings ('To confirm what we agreed...') so a shared record exists, and keep dated notes you could show a manager or HR.

Gaslighting.boundary_script: "I remember it differently, and I'm confident enough in my memory to say so. Let's look at the message. If we still disagree after that, I'd rather leave it there than be told I'm imagining things."
Gaslighting.safety_note: Being told your memory is wrong is not a physical-safety signal in itself. It becomes one when it travels with threats, monitoring, cutting off money or contact, or fear of what happens when you disagree. If any of that is present, talk to someone outside the relationship, such as a domestic abuse advocate, a counselor or a trusted friend, before confronting anything.
misuse_warning: Calling a one-off disagreement about a detail 'gaslighting' can shut down honest correction. The word fits a repeated pattern, not a single clash.
Using the label to win an argument or to wound someone turns a description of a pattern into a verdict.
Gaslighting.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Countering puts forward a rival version of events to win a point; gaslighting works on your trust in your own memory. Trivializing shrinks the importance of what you felt but accepts that it happened. Selective Memory is forgetting convenient facts, often passively, while gaslighting asserts the facts did not occur. If the live question is 'did this happen at all?', you are closer to gaslighting than to the others.

Astroturfing.short_definition: Making a campaign look like spontaneous public support when it is staged, funded or run by a hidden sponsor.
Astroturfing.core_meaning: Making a campaign look like spontaneous public support when it is staged, funded or run by a hidden sponsor.
Astroturfing.expanded_definition: Astroturfing is the staging of apparent grassroots support: letters, reviews, comments, rallies or accounts that look like independent members of the public but are organized by a concealed party. The name plays on AstroTurf, the artificial grass. What marks it is concealment of who stands behind the voices, not the use of organization or money, which real movements also use. It matters because people read the size of a crowd as evidence of what others believe.
Astroturfing.plain_language_summary: It looks like ordinary people agreeing on their own. In fact, someone hidden is running it and not telling you.
Astroturfing.why_this_matters: A view carries more weight when it looks like many ordinary people hold it, so a manufactured chorus crowds out the real one, and genuine grassroots voices then get doubted too.
what_it_is: Support presented as coming from unaffiliated people when a hidden sponsor, such as a company, agency or political group, is behind it.
Volume used in place of an argument: many apparent voices standing in for a case made on the merits.
Found in many settings, including public comment periods, product reviews, social media replies, letters to editors and petition drives.
Often a mix of real participants and staged ones, which makes the whole effort look more credible than it is.
what_it_sounds_like: Dozens of letters to a local paper that share the same unusual phrases.
A wave of five-star reviews posted within a few days, worded alike.
New social media accounts with few connections and a feed that pushes a single issue.
A 'concerned residents' group whose funding and staff are hard to find.
Public comment submissions bearing names of people who say they never wrote them.
Rally attendees who later say they were paid or bused in without being told who organized it.
what_it_is_not: A real movement that uses professional organizers, paid staff or a national network. Organization is not fakery.
A group that openly states who funds it and why.
People who independently hold the same view and use similar words because they read the same news story.
Supporters who were handed a sample letter and chose to sign and send it under their own names.
A business asking satisfied customers to leave honest reviews and saying so.
this_may_be_it_when: The people supposedly speaking cannot be found, or turn out not to exist.
The sponsor's role is hidden and surfaces only through leaks, filings or reporting.
Many messages match in wording, timing and structure across supposedly unconnected accounts.
Participants say they did not know what they were taking part in.
Independent investigators or regulators have documented the link between the sponsor and the voices.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The only evidence is that messages sound alike, which also happens when people share a news story.
The group is organized but openly says who runs it.
You have found one odd account, which is not a campaign.
The suspicion rests on disliking the cause rather than on anything shown about who is behind it.
You have seen only a screenshot and have not looked at the original source.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Neighbors who talk to one another often end up using the same phrases.
A popular cause can draw a large and genuinely spontaneous response, and size alone proves nothing.
Template letters supplied by an advocacy group are an openly used and long-standing practice.
common_false_positives: A hashtag that spreads fast because many real people care about the same event.
A well-funded charity campaign that names its funders on the front page.
Customers praising a shop in similar words because the shop is known for the same thing.
discernment_questions: Can you identify who is behind the campaign, and is that information easy to find?
Do the supposed individuals exist outside this campaign, with a history that predates it?
Would the message still persuade you if only five people were saying it instead of five hundred?
Is the wording suspiciously uniform, or only similar in the way a shared news story would produce?
Has a journalist, regulator or court looked into who organized it?
less_concerning_if: The sponsors are named openly and their interest is stated.
Participants can be reached and describe their own reasons in their own words.
Coverage by independent outlets confirms that real people showed up.
more_concerning_if: The sponsor stands to gain directly from the outcome and does not disclose that.
Voices appear in large numbers just before a decision date and vanish afterwards.
People who question the campaign are attacked or dismissed as outsiders instead of answered.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same messages reappear under different names after one set of accounts is removed.
Support swells ahead of votes or hearings and drops off immediately after.
Later reporting or filings reveal a funder or agency that was not mentioned at the start.
The apparent crowd mirrors the sponsor's talking points more closely than real local concerns.
Astroturfing.repair_check: Once the sponsor is exposed, watch whether they name themselves and take the staged material down, or rename the group and carry on. An organization that corrects the record says who paid for what.
Astroturfing.boundary_respect_check: Put one plain question to the campaign: who funds it? An open answer separates organizing from disguise. A reply that praises the cause and accuses you of attacking it is the opposite signal.
Astroturfing.psychological_mechanism: People use what others appear to think as a guide to what is safe and sensible to think themselves. A staged crowd borrows that habit, and it works better when the apparent supporters look like us. Asking who is behind a message weakens the effect.
Astroturfing.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe feeling out of step with a majority that turns out not to exist, dropping a view because it seems unpopular, or growing suspicious of every campaign afterwards, including honest ones. Cynicism can cost as much as being fooled.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the group a direct question in public: 'Who is funding this campaign?' Their answer, or the lack of one, tells you something.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to share or sign until you have found out who is behind it and confirmed that the people involved are real.
response_options.disengagement: Mute or step back from a thread that is flooded with near-identical posts, rather than arguing with accounts that may not be people.
response_options.support_seeking: Take a suspicious pattern to a reporter, a fact-checking service or the platform's reporting tool, with the examples you collected.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in communications, policy or moderation, record what you saw, with dates and examples, and follow your organization's process for reporting suspected coordinated activity.

Astroturfing.boundary_script: Verification script (to yourself, before sharing): "Who is actually behind this, can I find them, and would I still be persuaded if only five people were saying it instead of five hundred?"
Astroturfing.safety_note: Astroturfing is rarely a personal danger by itself. The risk to watch for is a campaign that targets named individuals with harassment, or that spreads their personal details. If that begins, save the evidence, report it to the platform, and speak to a lawyer or a local support service.
misuse_warning: Calling every large or noisy campaign astroturf is a way of dismissing real people who disagree with you. The claim needs evidence about who is behind it.
Accusing a named person of being a paid shill without proof can itself be a harmful smear.
Astroturfing.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent shapes what a whole society treats as normal through media and institutions, and it needs no fake voices. Computational Propaganda leans on bots and algorithms at scale, while astroturfing can be done with a few dozen paid or fake accounts. Normative Messaging uses real people's norms to nudge behavior openly. Astroturfing is the one built on voices that conceal who is behind them.
